report.currency: EUR (tables in € millions unless stated; ~US$ at EUR/USD 1.1212, 15 Oct 2026)
report.verdict: France's regulated market stalled in H1 2026: GGR excluding casinos rose just 0.5% to €5.66bn (~$6.35bn) as the two exclusive-rights monopolies (FDJ United lottery/retail, PMU horse racing) shrank and only the competitive online segment grew (+11% to €1.45bn / ~$1.62bn, now 25.6% of the market). The online growth is real but World Cup-loaded and bonus-fuelled (June stakes +47%, acquisition bonuses ×4, bonuses now 13.8% of online GGR) inside the heaviest tax regime in Europe (59.3% of GGR on online sports betting since 1 July 2025) and a regulator explicitly pushing for a "less intensive" model — a market for scale operators with disciplined CAC, not for opportunistic entrants.
summary: **Growth has stalled at the market level.** The ANJ's semi-annual review (published 15 Oct 2026) puts H1 2026 GGR (PBJ) excluding land-based casinos and Paris gaming clubs at €5.66bn (~$6.35bn), +0.5% YoY versus +4.1% in H1 2025. Casinos (€2.82bn / ~$3.16bn GGR in FY2025, +3.4%) are reported annually only, so the full-market run-rate is ~€14bn+ (FY2025: €14.1bn / ~$15.8bn, +3.0%).

**Online is the only growth engine.** Online GGR (sports betting, poker, horse racing — the only three products open to competition) rose 11.0% to €1,449m (~$1,625m), contributing +2.5pt to market growth, while FDJ United's exclusive-rights activities subtracted 1.2pt and PMU 0.8pt. Online penetration of the ex-casino market reached 25.6% (+2.4pt); on the FY2025 all-in base online was 18.5% (12.8% in 2019).

**Market structure remains a two-monopoly-plus-online model.** FDJ United's exclusive rights (lottery retail+online, retail sports betting) generated €3,429m (~$3,845m), 61% of ex-casino GGR; PMU's exclusive rights (pari-mutuel horse racing) €782m (~$877m), 13.8% share (15.8% in H1 2024); online sports betting €995m (~$1,116m), 17.6%; online poker €290m (~$325m); online horse racing €164m (~$184m).

**Sports betting growth was a June/World Cup event, not a trend.** Online sports stakes rose 10.6% to €6.62bn (~$7.42bn) and GGR 11.6% to €995m, but stakes grew only +4% in Jan–May versus +47% in June (€1,327m / ~$1,488m, 20% of the half's handle). Monthly active accounts rose +2% to +11% YoY in Jan–May, then +69% in June (3.14m). The ANJ itself frames H2 as the test of whether the World Cup durably widened the bettor pool.

**Promotional intensity is escalating faster than revenue.** Total online bonuses reached €199m (~$223m), +28% — 2.5× online GGR growth — and 13.8% of online GGR (11.9% a year earlier). Sports betting bonuses were €129m (~$145m, +35%; 12.9% of GGR vs 10.7%; ~1.9% of stakes); June alone absorbed €35.5m (vs €14.5m) and acquisition bonuses nearly quadrupled (€9.0m vs €2.4m). Poker was the exception: bonuses +11% (€50.9m) with acquisition spend −15%.

**Player base at a record, but monetisation per account is falling.** Online active accounts hit 5.85m (+24%) and unique players 4.06m (+17%); accounts per player rose from 1.37 to 1.44 and segments per player from 1.38 to 1.45 — players are spreading across more operators. Sports stakes per active account fell 14% (~€1,270), average bet slipped from €14.6 to €14.0, poker GGR per account fell 18% (€153→€126), horse racing GGR per account −3.7% (€312→€300).

**Poker is back in growth; horse racing online is volume-up, margin-down.** Poker GGR +13.4% to €290m, driven by Sit&Go (€202m, 70% of GGR; short formats +15.9%), with active accounts +38.5% to 2.3m — poker players are now 44% of all online unique players (38%). Online horse-race stakes rose 15.8% to €920m (~$1,032m), the strongest since 2021 and evenly spread across months, but GGR grew only 2.8% as hold fell from 20.1% to 17.8%.

**The monopolies are shrinking.** FDJ United's French exclusive-rights GGR fell 2.0% (−€69m), of which lottery −€64m (−2.1% to €2,979m / ~$3,340m; draw games −7.6% on fewer/lower EuroMillions jackpots and heatwave-hit retail footfall; +1% ex long EuroMillions cycles per the operator). Retail sports betting fell 1.1% to €450m (~$505m). PMU's stakes fell 3.8% to €3,096m (~$3,471m) and GGR 5.8% — a third straight decline, accelerating from −2.6% — with the stakes/GGR gap partly explained by PMU lifting the retail Simple bet RTP from 83.6% to 84.6% in Oct 2025.

**Licensing is a closed, three-product regime.** The ANJ (created 1 Jan 2020 under Ordinance 2019-1015, replacing ARJEL) licenses only online sports betting, online horse-race betting and online 'jeux de cercle' (poker). Each agrément is product-specific, granted for 5 years, renewable, non-transferable, and requires an EU/EEA seat. Fees are nominal (CGI art. 1012 / annex III art. 313 BR): €5k/€8k/€10k application for 1/2/3 licences and €20k/€30k/€40k annual. Online casino (slots, roulette, blackjack) remains illegal.

**Operator landscape: 16 licensed entities, with a visible wave of new entrants.** The ANJ register lists 16 licensees: 16 with sports betting, 5 with horse racing (Betclic, FDJ United's Unibet/Zeturf, Genybet, bet365, PMU) and 7 with poker (bwin/partypoker, Betclic, Unibet, bet365, PMU, PokerStars, Winamax). bet365.fr, betsson.fr, daznbet.fr, circusbet.fr and yesorno-jeu.fr are recent additions; FDJ United has unified its French online brands under Unibet. The ANJ does not publish operator market shares (n/a).

**Taxation is GGR-based and the heaviest in Europe, and it was raised on 1 July 2025 (LFSS 2025).** Online sports betting: 59.3% of GGR (33.7% state levy, CGI 302 bis ZH; 15.0% social levy, up from 10.6%; 10.6% national sports agency levy, CGI 1609 tricies), from 54.9%. Retail sports betting 42.1% (from 41.1%). Online poker: social levy moved from 0.2% of stakes to 10% of GGR. Online horse racing (incl. return to racing companies): 52.9% (from 52.3%). Lottery: 69% on jackpot draw games (from 68%), 56.5% on other draw/instant games (from 55.5%). FDJ United quantified the full-year hit at ~€90m revenue/EBITDA.

**Tax take is large and visible in operator accounts.** FDJ United reported €2,613m (~$2,930m) of public levies on €4,314m of group GGR in H1 2026 (+0.7% despite GGR −1.3%), and €52m of H1 revenue lost to 2025–26 tax increases (3pt of revenue growth). On the ANJ's online sports betting GGR of €995m, the 59.3% all-in rate implies ~€590m (~$662m) of H1 public levies [estimate]. Player winnings are untaxed online; land-based casino winnings above €1,500 bear a 13.7% social levy.

**Enforcement is active and expanding to new formats.** Since gaining administrative blocking powers (March 2022) the ANJ had blocked 1,337 illegal sites by late 2025, and in July 2026 obtained blocking of Polymarket, Stake and Cbet. The ANJ/PwC study sized illegal online GGR at €748m–€1.5bn (~$839m–$1,682m), 5–11% of the market; the industry lobby AFJEL's Nov 2025 barometer claims 5.4m players and €2bn (~$2.2bn) GGR — treat as advocacy, not regulator data.

**Responsible-gambling pressure is the dominant regulatory vector.** In May 2026 the ANJ published (Decision 2026-118) an algorithm to identify excessive/pathological players, stating ~600,000 online players show a high probability of excessive play, and expects operators to identify and support more of them. A July 2026 sanctions-commission decision (2026-031) addressed an operator's failures on excessive players, including bonus restrictions. The ANJ chair's FY2025 message was blunt: all indicators are 'red' and the framework needs adapting toward a less intensive model.

**Advertising is pre-controlled, not just policed.** Operators must submit annual promotional strategies and annual excessive-gambling action plans for ANJ approval (e.g., Decision 2026-016 for PMU), commercial communications are governed by Decree 2020-1349 with mandatory health warnings, and the ANJ can order withdrawal of ads. The 2023 influencer law restricts gambling promotion to age-gated platforms [framework not re-verified this session]. June's bonus surge shows the regime does not yet cap bonuses — a plausible next step.

**Payments are conventional and KYC-heavy.** Licensed operators run verified player accounts with mandatory self-set deposit and stake limits at account opening; withdrawals must go to a payment account in the player's name; cards and bank transfers dominate, crypto is not accepted by licensees [payments detail not re-verified this session — n/a for method shares].

**Online casino legalisation is stalled.** A PLF 2025 amendment (Oct 2024) proposing a 55.6%-of-GGR tax on online casino was withdrawn within days under land-based casino pressure; the Bercy consultation launched Nov 2024 has not resumed and no bill was on the 2026 agenda. A March 2026 IGF report reportedly favours a conditional opening [unverified]. Expect the debate to recur in the PLF/PLFSS 2027 cycle; nothing before 2027 at the earliest.

**Structural adjacencies:** Paris gaming clubs (FY2025 GGR €97m / ~$109m, −21% after two months' closure) were made permanent after an eight-year experiment; the JONUM (monetisable digital objects / Web3 games) experimental framework took effect early 2026; the ANJ's 14 Oct 2026 note on 2025 online sports betting linked niche football leagues to excessive bettors — a signal that content restrictions ('liste sport') may tighten.

**Operator read-through for B2Tech.** France is a large, low-growth, high-tax, high-compliance market where the addressable (competitive) pool is ~€2.9bn annualised online GGR, growing ~9–11%, split among 16 licensees with escalating bonus inflation. Entry is cheap on fees but expensive on marketing and margin (59.3% levy leaves ~€0.41 of each GGR euro before costs). The investable thesis is scale and CAC discipline in sports/poker; horse racing is a niche with eroding hold; online casino is not an option; and the political direction (tax, RG, advertising) is uniformly tighter.

segments.name: Online sports betting
segments.headline: +11.6% GGR to €995m, but a June/World Cup spike (stakes +47%) bought with a near-quadrupling of acquisition bonuses; Jan–May stakes grew only 4%.
narrative: Online sports betting stakes reached €6,616m (~$7,418m) in H1 2026, +10.6%, and GGR €995m (~$1,116m), +11.6%, on a hold of 15.0% (14.9% in H1 2025, 15.2% in H1 2024). The ANJ's monthly annex shows how uneven the half was: hold swung from 20.3% in January and May to 11.4% in February and 12.2% in June, when World Cup results favoured punters (FDJ United separately reported 'high' player-return rates on the tournament). Q1 stakes were €3,192m and Q2 €3,425m; June alone was €1,327m (~$1,488m), 20% of the half's handle, versus a Jan–May run-rate of ~€1,060m a month. The segment is still the engine of the online market, contributing 7.9 of the 11 points of online GGR growth, and now holds 68.6% of online GGR.

The player data point to a recruitment surge rather than deepening engagement. Active accounts rose 28% to 5.2m and unique players 21% to 3.6m, but monthly active accounts grew only +2% to +11% YoY from January to May before jumping +69% in June to 3.14m. Stakes per active account fell 14% to roughly €1,270 for the half, the average bet slipped from €14.6 to €14.0 (and from €17.4 to €14.7 in June), and the number of bets totalled ~469m. Accounts per player rose to 1.43, consistent with newer entrants (bet365, Betsson, DAZN Bet, Circus) prying open multi-accounting. The ANJ's own caveat — that H2 activity will show whether the pool has durably widened — is the right one; our prior from Euro 2024 and the 2022 World Cup is that a majority of event-recruited accounts churn within two quarters.

Promotional spend is the structural concern for any operator's unit economics. Bonuses paid to sports bettors reached €129m (~$145m), +35%, equal to 12.9% of GGR (10.7%) and ~1.9% of stakes; June took €35.5m (28% of the half) against €14.5m in June 2025, and acquisition bonuses, down 6% from January to May, were multiplied by almost four in June (€9.0m vs €2.4m). With all-in public levies at 59.3% of GGR, a 12.9% bonus ratio leaves roughly 28% of GGR for all other costs before margin — the market is being competed on CAC, not product. A 15.0%-hold month like January can mask this; a 12% June cannot.

Product mix shifted with the calendar. Football took 55.8% of stakes (53.1%), rising 16% over the half with +116% in June and only +2.5% Jan–May; excluding June its share actually slipped (54% vs 55%). Tennis, the growth driver of 2025, stagnated (+2% Jan–May) and fell 13.5% in June, its share dropping from 26.0% to 23.2%. Basketball held 8.5% (9.1%), rugby 1.6% (1.9%) and other sports 11.0% (10.0%), with 'other sports' stakes +21% — the only organic diversification signal. Live betting's share of stakes was flat at 50% from January to May but fell from 54% to 44% in June, as tournament pre-match volume dominated.

Regulatory read-through: three days before this report the ANJ published a note on 2025 online sports betting linking niche football leagues to excessive bettors, and its May 2026 excessive-player algorithm is now in operators' hands. The combination of a bonus-driven World Cup, a 13% bonus/GGR ratio and a regulator asking for a 'less intensive' model makes bonus restrictions (by promotional-strategy approval if not by decree) the most probable near-term rule change for this segment. Operators modelling France should assume promotional headroom narrows from 2027, and that FY2026 segment GGR of roughly €1.95–2.0bn (~$2.2bn) [estimate: FY2025 €1,766m plus H1 growth and a July World Cup final] is a peak-cycle base, not a trend line.

segments.name: Online poker & online horse-race betting
segments.headline: Poker returned to double-digit growth (+13.4%) on Sit&Go and a 38% jump in accounts; horse racing online posted its best stakes growth since 2021 (+15.8%) but hold fell to 17.8%.
narrative: Online poker GGR reached €290m (~$325m), +13.4%, after a flat H1 2025 (−0.4%), and contributed 2.6 points of online growth. Almost all of the increase came from short formats: Sit&Go (nearly all variable-prize 'expresso'-type) generated €202m, 70% of segment GGR, and Sit&Go plus MTT together rose 15.9% to €240m (83% of GGR); cash game stabilised at ~€50m (+2.8% after −14%). The monthly annex shows Sit&Go GGR accelerating through the half — +5–10% YoY in Q1, ~+20% in April–May, ~+30% in June — which suggests cross-sell from the World Cup sports audience into lottery-like poker formats rather than a poker-native revival. Poker's share of online GGR recovered to 20.0% (19.6%).

Poker's player base expanded far faster than its revenue: active accounts +38.5% to 2.3m and unique players +34.4% to 1.8m, three times the growth rates of H1 2025, with monthly accounts up 16% in January–February, 21–29% in March–May and 62% in June. GGR per active account fell 18% from €153 to €126. Poker players now represent 44% of all online unique players (38%). Unlike sports betting, this growth was not bonus-led: segment bonuses rose 11% to €50.9m (17.6% of GGR), slower than GGR, acquisition bonuses fell 15%, and bonus per account dropped from €27 to €22. Seven operators hold poker licences (bwin/partypoker, Betclic, Unibet, bet365, PMU, PokerStars, Winamax); liquidity is ring-fenced to France apart from the shared-liquidity arrangements permitted since 2018.

The tax change matters more for poker than any other product. From 1 July 2025 the social levy moved from 0.2% of stakes to 10% of GGR (LFSS 2025), so H1 2026 is the first half fully under the new base. Growth of +13.4% despite this suggests operators have not passed the cost through in rake; whether margins absorbed it is not visible in ANJ data. Against land-based casinos (whose social levies rose only 0.7pt) the industry argued the change created a competitive distortion; against the illegal online casino market (ANJ/PwC: €748m–€1.5bn GGR) it widens the pricing gap further.

Online horse-race betting stakes rose 15.8% to €920m (~$1,032m), the strongest growth since 2021 (+6% in H1 2024, +1% in H1 2025), with every month up 13–20% YoY and no June peak. GGR, however, grew only 2.8% to €164m (~$184m) as hold fell from 20.1% to 17.8% — a two-point give-back that mirrors PMU's own RTP increase in its retail network and points to price competition for the same pari-mutuel pools. Active accounts rose 6.8% to 547k and unique players 3.2% to 462k, so growth is activity per player (GGR per account nonetheless −3.7% to €300). Galop stakes grew 18.2% to €456m and trot 13.5% to €464m, near parity, with trot dominating winter months (~60% in Jan–Feb) and galop spring (~55% Mar–May). Bonuses rose 36% to €19.7m, 12.0% of GGR (9.1%), 96% of it retention.

Commercial implication: the online horse-racing channel is taking share from PMU's physical network (online now 23% of horse-race stakes vs 20% a year earlier) but with five licensees (Betclic, Unibet/Zeturf, Genybet, bet365, PMU) competing on returns in pools whose economics are set by the racing companies' levy (public levies incl. the racing return ~52.9% of GGR per FDJ United). This is a scale-and-content niche: attractive for an operator that already runs pari-mutuel or racing media, marginal otherwise. Poker is the more interesting adjacency for a sportsbook-led entrant — it is growing, under-bonused and benefits from cross-sell — but the 10%-of-GGR social levy plus the French state poker levy [rate unverified] set a hard floor on rake.

segments.name: Exclusive-rights operators: FDJ United (lottery & retail sports betting) and PMU (horse racing)
segments.headline: The monopolies that still hold 75% of ex-casino GGR both contracted — FDJ United −2.0% on a weak EuroMillions cycle and heatwaves, PMU −5.8% in a third straight year of decline.
narrative: FDJ United's activities under exclusive rights in France generated €3,429m (~$3,845m) of GGR in H1 2026, −2.0% (−€69m), after contributing 2.7 points to market growth a year earlier. Lottery accounted for €64m of the decline (−2.1% to €2,979m / ~$3,340m): draw games fell 7.6% because, in the operator's words, high EuroMillions jackpots were fewer and lower than in 2025, and Q2 retail footfall suffered from heatwaves; excluding long EuroMillions cycles (jackpots above €75m) the operator says lottery GGR rose 1%. Retail sports betting — FDJ's second monopoly — fell 1.1% to €450m (~$505m) with Q2 improving on a more attractive offer. At group level (including Kindred's European online business and Irish lottery) GGR was €4,314m (~$4,837m), −1.3%; public levies were €2,613m (~$2,930m), +0.7%; net gaming revenue €1,701m (−4.1%); revenue €1,782m (~$1,998m), −4.5%, of which €52m (3pt) was lost to 2025–26 tax increases in France, the UK, the Netherlands and Romania.

Profitability and guidance frame what the French tax regime does to even a monopoly. Recurring EBITDA fell 8.4% to €404m (~$453m), a 22.7% margin (23.6%), and recurring operating profit 15.1% to €229m; the reported net result swung from a €136m profit to a €16m loss on €135m of impairments on online betting and gaming intangibles (Netherlands, UK, Romania regulatory changes) plus a €20m exceptional contribution on large-company profits. Net debt was stable at €1,964m and Moody's reaffirmed Baa1. FDJ United now guides to stable FY2026 GGR in both its French network and online BUs, a low-single-digit revenue decline, a 23–24% EBITDA margin, a dividend payout of at least 75% of adjusted net income, and has opened a review of its online markets and non-core payments assets. The ANJ notes that the market's full-year trajectory depends on FDJ United, which is 61% of ex-casino GGR. Its online BU (France, Nordics, UK, NL etc.) held GGR flat at €702m; excluding the Netherlands and UK, GGR grew 6.6% 'notably' on France — a reminder that FDJ United is also the largest-capitalised competitor in the open online market under the Unibet brand.

PMU's exclusive-rights (pari-mutuel) business is in structural retreat. Stakes fell 3.8% to €3,096m (~$3,471m) — a third consecutive decline after −2% (H1 2024) and −4.2% (H1 2025), and €264m (−7.9%) lower than two years ago — and the decline was evenly spread across Q1 (−3.9%) and Q2 (−3.7%) rather than front-loaded as in 2025. GGR fell faster, −5.8% to €782m (~$877m), with the acceleration concentrated in Q2 (−5.7% vs −1.3% a year earlier); network GGR is down €70m (−8.2%) in two years. The ANJ attributes part of the stakes/GGR gap to PMU raising the return to player on its retail Simple bet from 83.6% to 84.6% from October 2025 — i.e. PMU is buying volume defence with margin. PMU's share of the ex-casino market fell to 13.8% (15.8% in H1 2024, 14.7% in H1 2025), and online sports betting, which overtook it in H1 2025, is now 3.8 points ahead. PMU's network still carries over three-quarters of all horse-race stakes, but its share slipped from 80% to 77% as online horse-race stakes grew 15.8% (PMU also competes online via pmu.fr).

Governance and funding of the racing ecosystem are now the policy issue. 2026 is a transition year: Cyrille Giraudat became CEO in January 2026, Éric Woerth (a former budget minister) was appointed chair on 30 March 2026, and a 'Pacte PMU 2030' is being drafted. The 2026 budget adopted on 30 June provides €725m (~$813m) for the horse-racing industry, down from €802m (~$899m) in 2025 (−9.6%); FY2025 had already shown stakes −3.3% to €6.4bn, GGR −2.8% to €1,651m and a player base down 5.7% to 3.3m. For an operator, the relevant implications are (i) the racing companies' levy on online horse-race betting is set annually by decree and can rise to compensate the filière, and (ii) PMU's political weight — rural retail network, racing employment — makes any liberalisation of pari-mutuel exclusivity improbable.

Land-based casinos and clubs sit outside the semi-annual report but shape the online-casino debate. FY2025 casino GGR was €2,816m (~$3,157m), +3.4%, on 31.6m entries (+2%); the Paris gaming clubs, finally made permanent after an eight-year experiment, posted €97m (~$109m), −21%, after a two-month closure. The land-based sector's successful October 2024 lobbying against the online-casino amendment and its FY2025 recovery mean its opposition to iGaming legalisation is undiminished; any future opening is likely to be designed around land-based licence holders (the ANJ itself has advocated a 'highly controlled' approach).

segments.name: Licensing, taxation & operator landscape
segments.headline: Cheap to license, brutal to tax: 16 licensees compete for three online products under a 59.3%-of-GGR regime for sports betting that was raised in July 2025 and sits in a budget cycle hunting for revenue.
narrative: The legal architecture dates from Law 2010-476 (12 May 2010), which opened online sports betting, online horse-race betting and online poker to competition under ARJEL, and Ordinance 2019-1015 (2 Oct 2019), which created the Autorité nationale des jeux (ANJ) from 1 Jan 2020 with authority over the whole sector: the online licensees, FDJ (whose lottery and retail sports-betting exclusivity was secured for 25 years under the 2019 PACTE privatisation), PMU (retail pari-mutuel horse racing), and — for responsible-gambling and advertising oversight — land-based casinos and clubs. Everything not expressly authorised is prohibited: online casino games, online bingo and betting exchanges remain illegal, and the ANJ polices the perimeter via administrative blocking.

An agrément is issued per product category (paris sportifs, paris hippiques, jeux de cercle), for five years, renewable, non-transferable, and only to operators with a registered seat in the EU/EEA; it is conditional on a detailed cahier des charges, a certified technical platform with data archiving accessible to the ANJ (the 'frontal'), and player-protection obligations. Fees are trivial relative to market size (CGI art. 1012 and annex III art. 313 BR): €5,000 / €8,000 / €10,000 at application for one / two / three categories and €20,000 / €30,000 / €40,000 a year. The real cost of entry is operating: monthly levy declarations, ANJ pre-approval of the annual promotional strategy and the excessive-gambling action plan, AML obligations and the five-yearly renewal (recent examples: Zeturf's sports licence renewed 14 May 2024; PMU's sports licence renewed June 2025).

The ANJ register (October 2026) lists 16 licensed entities. All 16 hold sports-betting licences; five hold horse-race licences (Betclic, FDJ Online Betting and Gaming France [unibet.fr/zeturf.fr], Genybet, Hillside [bet365.fr], PMU) and seven hold poker licences (B.E.S. [bwin.fr/partypoker.fr], Betclic, FDJ Online B&G France, Hillside, PMU, Reel Malta [PokerStars], Winamax). The notable change since 2024 is the arrival of international brands — bet365.fr, betsson.fr, daznbet.fr (BCFR4), circusbet.fr (BCFR2) — plus niche entrants (feelingbet.fr, olybet.fr, vbet.fr, netbet.fr, yesorno-jeu.fr), and FDJ United's unification of its French online brands under Unibet after absorbing Kindred. The ANJ does not publish operator shares; trade consensus places Winamax, Betclic and Unibet as the sports-betting leaders [unverified], and the ANJ's data on rising accounts-per-player (1.37→1.44) is consistent with new entrants buying trial via bonuses.

Taxation is levied on GGR (PBJ) for every vertical since the 2020 reform (poker's social levy was the last stakes-based element, converted on 1 July 2025). For online sports betting the all-in public take is 59.3% of GGR — 33.7% state levy (CGI 302 bis ZH), 15.0% social levy (CSS L137-21, raised from 10.6% by LFSS 2025 art. 32) and 10.6% levy for the Agence nationale du sport (CGI 1609 tricies) — the highest headline rate in Europe. Retail sports betting pays 42.1% (41.1% before), online horse-race betting 52.9% including the racing companies' return (52.3%), online poker a 10%-of-GGR social levy (from 0.2% of stakes; the separate state levy on poker stakes is not re-verified here), lottery 69% on jackpot draw games and 56.5% on other draw/instant games (each +1pt via CSG 6.2%→7.2%), and casinos a progressive state levy on GGR plus social levies that rose ~0.7pt [scale unverified]. Player winnings are untaxed online; land-based casino winnings above €1,500 bear a 13.7% social levy, and amendments to extend that to betting and lottery (estimated €200m a year) have been tabled, not adopted. Operators pay in addition the ordinary corporate income tax and, for FDJ United in 2026, the exceptional contribution on large-company profits.

The commercial consequence is a margin stack that only scale survives. On H1 2026 online sports betting GGR of €995m, statutory levies imply ~€590m (~$662m) of public take [estimate], leaving ~€405m for the whole licensed sector before bonuses (€129m), payment and platform costs, content and staff — roughly €0.28 of each GGR euro before marketing media and overhead. FDJ United quantified the 1 July 2025 increases at ~€45m in 2025 and ~€90m in a full year and says it will take until 2027 to offset them; AFJEL warned of exits among smaller licensees. We have not yet seen exits, but we have seen bonus inflation and hold compression in horse racing. Direction of travel: the 2025 budget cycle established gambling as a go-to revenue line; with the 2026 budget adopted only in February 2026 after a protracted process [secondary], the PLFSS/PLF 2027 debates this autumn are the next window for further levy or winnings-tax changes — the key regulatory swing factor for FY2027 planning.

segments.name: Enforcement, responsible gambling, advertising, payments & the online-casino question
segments.headline: The ANJ is tightening on every axis — blocking (1,337 sites, now Polymarket/Stake), an excessive-player algorithm flagging ~600k accounts, sanctions tied to bonuses — while online casino legalisation stays frozen.
narrative: Enforcement against unlicensed supply has hardened since the ANJ obtained administrative (non-judicial) blocking and de-listing powers in March 2022: by late 2025 it reported 1,337 illegal gambling sites blocked, and in July 2026 it secured the blocking in France of Polymarket (prediction markets treated as unlicensed betting), Stake and Cbet. The regulator's own sizing of the illegal online market (ANJ/PwC study) is €748m–€1.5bn (~$839m–$1,682m) of GGR, 5–11% of the total market — dominated by online casino, which is illegal in France. The industry lobby AFJEL's November 2025 barometer claims 5.4m French players and €2bn (~$2.2bn) of illegal GGR, i.e. a black market now larger than the licensed online market, with €1.2bn of foregone tax; those figures are advocacy for legalising online casino and should be weighted accordingly. For a licensed operator the practical reading is that channelisation in sports betting and poker is high, while slot/casino demand leaks entirely offshore.

Responsible gambling has become the ANJ's primary lever and it is moving from principles to measurement. The 2024–2026 strategic plan placed reduction of excessive gambling at the centre; on 26 May 2026 the ANJ published Decision 2026-118, releasing to operators an algorithm for identifying excessive or pathological players and stating that roughly 600,000 online players have a high probability of being excessive — against 4.06m unique players, that is ~15% of the base. Operators are expected to identify numbers 'consistent with the size of their player pool', contact them, impose moderators, refer them to support and, as a last resort, close accounts. The sanctions commission's Decision 2026-031 (10 July 2026) fined an operator over failures on this duty, and the remedies recorded include ceasing monthly loyalty bonuses to excessive players — the first explicit link between bonus policy and sanction. Existing hard rules: mandatory self-set deposit and stake limits at account opening, a national self-exclusion register (~86,000 people in 2025 [ANJ brochure, approximate]), bans on credit, annual ANJ-approved action plans per operator (e.g. Decision 2026-016, PMU), and the ANJ-run 'Evalujeu' self-assessment.

Advertising is pre-controlled rather than merely policed. Decree 2020-1349 (4 Nov 2020) governs commercial communications — no targeting of minors, no association of gambling with social or financial success, mandatory health warnings — and each operator must obtain ANJ approval of its annual promotional strategy, with the ANJ empowered to order withdrawal of non-compliant communications; the 2023 influencer law confines gambling promotion to age-gated platforms [framework not re-verified this session]. The H1 2026 data will embarrass that framework: acquisition bonuses nearly quadrupled in June, total online bonuses reached 13.8% of GGR, and the ANJ had already warned before the tournament that 41% of French World Cup viewers intended to bet [trade-press report of an ANJ note]. We expect the ANJ to use 2027 promotional-strategy approvals to constrain bonus volumes and World Cup-style acquisition bursts, and the chair's call for 'adaptations to the regulatory framework' to translate into a bonus cap or a ban on bonuses for flagged players.

Payments in the licensed market are conventional. Each player holds a verified account with a single operator per licence; withdrawals must be made to a payment account in the player's own name; deposits are by bank card, bank transfer and regulated e-wallets/prepaid vouchers, with no credit and no crypto accepted by licensees [method shares n/a — not published by the ANJ]. There is no mobile-money layer as in African markets; the operational friction is KYC (identity and bank-account verification before withdrawal) and AML reporting to TRACFIN, not payment acceptance. Winnings are untaxed in players' hands for online betting and poker, which supports channelisation.

The online-casino question remains the structural gap. An amendment to the PLF 2025 tabled in October 2024 would have legalised online casino with a 55.6%-of-GGR tax (aligned with online lottery) and was withdrawn within about ten days after land-based casinos mobilised; the Bercy consultation that replaced it held a first plenary in November 2024, promised conclusions in Q1 2025, and has not resumed following the government's fall. As of April 2026 the ANJ confirmed the process was still suspended; a March 2026 Inspection générale des finances report is said to favour a conditional opening on a Belgian-style model [unverified], and no bill is scheduled for 2026. Realistically the earliest vehicle is the 2027 budget, with land-based licence holders likely to be structurally advantaged in any design. Adjacent frameworks are moving faster: the JONUM (Web3 monetisable digital objects) experimental regime took effect in early 2026 and the Paris gaming clubs were made permanent; neither offers a route to online slots.

highlights.text: Competitive online pool is large and still compounding: €1,449m (~$1,625m) GGR in H1 2026, +11% (vs +8.2% in H1 2025), on an FY2025 base of €2,617m; with all three products growing for the first time in several years, FY2026 online GGR of ~€2.85–2.9bn (~$3.2bn) is plausible [estimate].

Record and diversifying player base: 5.85m active accounts (+24%) and 4.06m unique players (+17%), with accounts-per-player up to 1.44 — new brands can win trial, as bet365, Betsson and DAZN Bet have shown since 2025.

Poker is an under-bonused growth adjacency: GGR +13.4% with acquisition bonuses −15%, Sit&Go accelerating to ~+30% YoY by June and poker players now 44% of online uniques — cross-sell economics favour a sportsbook-plus-poker licence pair.

Monopoly erosion creates share: PMU's share fell to 13.8% (15.8% two years ago) and online horse-race stakes +15.8% are migrating pari-mutuel volume to licensed online books; FDJ retail sports betting (−1.1%) continues to lose relative ground to online.

Licensing cost is negligible and the perimeter is legally clear: €5–10k application, €20–40k annual, 5-year renewable agréments, no local-ownership or server-location mandates beyond an EU/EEA seat and ANJ-accessible archiving.

High channelisation in licensed products: untaxed player winnings, a 1,337-site blocking record and the July 2026 Polymarket/Stake orders keep sports and poker demand onshore, limiting black-market price competition in those verticals.

World Cup 2026 showed the market still responds to events: June stakes +47%, 3.14m monthly actives (+69%), FDJ United group tournament stakes >€700m — the H2 retention data (FY report ~April 2027) will tell operators the true event ROI.

lowlights.text: Highest tax burden in Europe and rising: 59.3% of GGR on online sports betting since 1 July 2025 (from 54.9%), poker social levy now 10% of GGR, and gambling has become a recurring revenue line in a strained budget cycle — PLFSS/PLF 2027 is a live risk for further increases or a winnings tax.

Bonus inflation is outrunning revenue: online bonuses +28% to €199m, 13.8% of GGR; sports bonuses 12.9% of GGR and acquisition spend ×~4 in June — a CAC war among 16 licensees on a 41%-of-GGR net base.
Growth is event-dependent and per-account monetisation is falling: Jan–May sports stakes only +4%; stakes per active account −14%; poker GGR per account −18%; horse-racing hold down 2.3pt to 17.8%.

Regulatory direction is uniformly restrictive: ANJ algorithm flags ~600k excessive players (~15% of uniques), a July 2026 sanction tied remedies to bonus withdrawal, the chair calls for a 'less intensive' model, and the Oct 2026 niche-leagues note points to tighter content rules — expect bonus caps and marketing constraints from the 2027 promotional-strategy cycle.

No online casino, and no credible path before 2027: the 2024 amendment was withdrawn, the Bercy consultation is dormant, land-based casinos (FY2025 GGR €2.8bn, +3.4%) remain opposed — the ~€0.75–1.5bn (regulator) to €2bn (industry) of casino demand stays offshore.

Monopoly incumbents are also the best-capitalised competitors: FDJ United (61% of ex-casino GGR, €1.96bn net debt, Baa1) runs Unibet in the open market and PMU holds all three online licences; both have political weight in setting racing levies and content lists.

Horse racing economics are deteriorating for everyone: online hold fell from 20.1% to 17.8%, PMU raised retail RTP by 1pt, the racing industry's funding was cut 9.6% to €725m — pressure to raise the racing companies' levy (set by decree) on online operators is the likely response.

forecast.intro: The market bridge from H1 2025 to H1 2026 is simple and uncomfortable: headline growth fell from +4.1% to +0.5% because the two exclusive-rights operators swung from contributing +2.7pt (FDJ United alone, H1 2025) to subtracting 2.0pt combined (FDJ United −1.2pt on a weak EuroMillions cycle and heatwaves; PMU −0.8pt on a structural, accelerating decline), while the competitive online segment lifted its contribution to +2.5pt (sports betting +11.6%, poker +13.4%, horse racing +2.8%) — but with a June that supplied most of the sports growth on a near-quadrupling of acquisition bonuses. FY2025 context: the full market grew 3.0% to €14.1bn (~$15.8bn) with online at 18.5%; FDJ United now guides to flat FY2026 French-network GGR and the ANJ flags that full-year online growth depends on post-World Cup retention of a record 5.85m active accounts.

bridge.title: PMU exclusive rights → H1 2026 market growth

forecast.view: **Market:** we expect FY2026 ex-casino GGR of roughly €11.2–11.4bn (~$12.6–12.8bn), flat to +1% [estimate], with FDJ United's H2 lottery promotional push offsetting PMU's continued −3% to −5% slide, and online GGR of ~€2.85–2.9bn (+9–11%) [estimate] as the July World Cup final adds to Q3 before a tougher Q4 comparison; online penetration should end 2026 above 26% of the ex-casino market and above 20% all-in. **Margins:** the 59.3% levy is fixed for 2026 but operator economics will be squeezed by bonus inflation (we expect bonuses to stay above 13% of online GGR for the year) and by hold normalisation after an unusually strong January/May; expect at least one smaller licensee to exit or be acquired within 18 months, and consolidation around Winamax, Betclic, Unibet/FDJ United, bet365 and PMU. **Regulation:** the base case is no new levy increase in the 2027 budget but a non-trivial (one-in-three) risk of either a further social-levy step or an extension of the 13.7% winnings levy to betting/lottery; the ANJ will tighten promotional-strategy approvals for 2027 (bonus volume ceilings, restrictions on bonuses to flagged players, event-period limits) and push adoption of its excessive-player algorithm with sanctions as the enforcement tool; online casino legalisation remains off the table until at least the PLF 2027 debate, with any eventual design favouring land-based licence holders. **Leverage/structure:** PMU's 'Pacte PMU 2030' and the −9.6% cut in racing funding make an increase in the racing companies' levy on online horse-race betting (by decree) more likely than any liberalisation; FDJ United's review of its online markets could bring portfolio sales but not a retreat from France. Net: France is a mature, slow-growing, high-tax market that rewards scale, CAC discipline and compliance capacity — attractive as a top-up for an established European operator, unattractive as a greenfield entry.
watch: PLFSS/PLF 2027 debates (autumn 2026 – early 2027): any change to the 15% social levy on online sports betting, the 10% poker levy, or extension of the 13.7% winnings levy to betting and lottery.

ANJ FY2026 market review (~April 2027) and the H2 2026 retention of the 5.85m active accounts and 3.14m June monthly actives — the real World Cup ROI test; also FDJ United's Q3 revenue (21 Oct 2026) for the first read on post-tournament lottery and online trends.

ANJ 2027 promotional-strategy approvals and any decree or guideline capping bonuses or restricting them to flagged players, following Decision 2026-118 (algorithm) and sanctions Decision 2026-031; further sanctions naming operators.
Online casino: any restart of the Bercy consultation, publication of the IGF report, or a PLF 2027 amendment; land-based casino sector positioning.
PMU 'Pacte PMU 2030' (governance under Giraudat/Woerth), the 2027 racing-funding budget and the annual decree setting the racing companies' levy on online horse-race betting.
ANJ action on content: evolution of the authorised 'liste sport' after the Oct 2026 note on niche football leagues and excessive bettors; further blocking of prediction-market platforms.
Licence cycle: new applications (post-bet365/Betsson/DAZN wave) and 2027 five-year renewals; any exits among smaller sports-only licensees under the 59.3% regime.
